- **Food-grade lubricant** — essential, not optional, for reassembly. As one supplier notes, this lube is used for 
lubricating drive shafts and seals, freezer door O-rings and gaskets, pump parts and high-friction components
. Never reassemble dry; it accelerates wear on exactly the seals you've already been dealing with.
- **A soft brush** (for the drive coupling/rear bearing area we discussed as a common hidden buildup spot)
- **Clean sanitizing basin/solution** and rinse water
- **Small flathead or the adjustment screw tool** for the beater door adjustment screw (5/16-24 thread noted in the parts list)
- **Clean lint-free cloths**

### Tier 2: What you actually need given your current diagnostics (motor/gearbox/contactor level)

Since you're past routine cleaning and into winding resistance tests, contactor checks, and gearbox alignment, you'll want a proper tool kit on hand before you pull the assembly this time:

**Electrical/diagnostic**
- **Multimeter with resistance/continuity mode** (minimum) — for the winding resistance test we discussed
- **Megohmmeter**, if available, for a proper insulation resistance test — recall the safety note that if it lacks a discharge function, you should 
connect the tested device to ground via a 5 kW, 5 W resistor
 before handling
- **Clamp meter** (you already have this)
- **Insulated screwdriver** for capacitor discharge, plus insulated gloves as a backup safety layer

**Mechanical**
- **Standard nut driver/socket set** (Taylor assemblies commonly use hex-head hardware for door and motor mount fasteners)
- **Phillips and flathead screwdrivers**, various sizes
- **Adjustable wrench or specific-size wrench set** for gearbox mounting bolts, given the alignment check involves 
loosening bolts and tightening one bolt at a time
 to reset the gearbox coupling position
- **Torque wrench**, if you have one — reassembling the gearbox coupling to spec matters for the alignment issue we discussed
- **Feeler gauges**, useful if you need to check shaft/coupling clearance during the gearbox alignment inspection

**Safety/prep**
- **Lockout/tagout** for the breaker, given you'll have the motor compartment open with power considerations
- **Gloves** (cut-resistant for handling blades/edges, and separately, electrically insulated ones for capacitor work)
- **A container/tray for small parts and hardware** — o-rings, screws, and pins are easy to lose track of once several subassemblies are apart at once

### One practical note specific to your situation

Since you'll have the assembly open anyway for the winding/contactor checks, this is a good opportunity to do several of the outstanding items in one session rather than repeated teardowns: inspect the drive coupling for buildup, check the gearbox alignment, and do a final visual on scraper blade wear — all while you already have things disassembled for the electrical tests. Have fresh o-rings, scraper blades, and lubricant on hand as consumables before you start, so a single teardown can also double as the replacement if any of those come back worn.

script.question: Could a worn drive belt or coupling cause similar symptoms to a beater motor issue?
script.answer:
Good question to clarify, and it also corrects an assumption worth addressing directly: **Taylor soft-serve machines like the C708 don't use a drive belt at all** — the beater motor connects to the beater shaft through a direct **gearbox and hex drive coupling**, not a belt-and-pulley system. So "worn belt" isn't actually a failure mode on this machine, but a worn or damaged **coupling** absolutely can produce symptoms nearly identical to a motor fault — which is important, because it means your winding-resistance-clean motor could still be the source of your overload trips through this exact path.

### How a worn coupling mimics a motor issue

The hex coupling connects the gearbox output to the beater shaft. Several documented coupling failure modes are called out specifically for this machine family:

**Rounded corners on the coupling or shaft**
One troubleshooting source flags this directly: 
see if the drive shaft, coupling or both have rounded corners
, listed right alongside gearbox misalignment as a cause of drive-shaft-stuck symptoms. A hex coupling with rounded edges (from wear or over-torquing over time) starts to slip under load instead of transmitting full torque cleanly — this can manifest as the motor working harder to achieve the same beater rotation, which shows up as elevated current, exactly mimicking a motor winding or capacitor problem.

**Buildup in the coupling itself**
We touched on this earlier, but it bears repeating in this context: 
mix and lubricant buildup is in the drive coupling
 can physically restrict how freely the coupling engages, adding drag that the motor has to overcome — again, indistinguishable from a motor problem using amp draw alone.

**Rear shell bearing wear**
Closely related to the coupling (they sit in the same assembly area), a 
worn rear-shell bearing
 increases friction right at the point where the motor's output shaft meets the drive train, adding resistance the motor has to fight through on every rotation.

### Why this matters for your specific diagnostic sequence

This is exactly why the recommended troubleshooting order matters: an elevated amp reading (like your 4.2A) can be caused by problems on *either side* of that motor-to-coupling connection — a genuinely weak motor, or a perfectly healthy motor being forced to work against a degraded coupling. Your winding resistance test only clears the motor itself; it says nothing about the coupling. This is precisely why the gearbox/coupling alignment check was already on your list as a separate step, not a redundant one — a clean motor test result doesn't rule this out.

### What to check specifically at the coupling

- Visually inspect the hex coupling's corners/edges for rounding or wear against the shaft profile
- Check for any play or slop when you try to rotate the coupling by hand relative to the shaft (should be a tight, positive fit)
- Clean and inspect for the lubricant/mix buildup noted above
- Confirm the rear shell bearing has no excessive mix leakage into the drip pan, which is one indicator of that bearing failing

Given you'll likely have the assembly open for the winding/contactor checks anyway, this coupling inspection fits naturally into that same teardown session.

script.question: Is there a daily checklist that would help catch these issues earlier?
script.answer:
Let me check if there's an actual Taylor-published daily checklist to anchor this against, rather than just synthesizing our own.
Yes — and given everything we've walked through, a daily checklist is exactly the right next move since almost every fault we've discussed (BEATER OVERLOAD, HPCO, dull blades, coupling wear) gives early warning signs before it fully trips. Taylor's own operator manual for this platform includes a "Regular Maintenance Checks" section, and I've combined that with everything specific to your troubleshooting history below.

### Daily — Opening

- **Visual check of scraper blades** for nicks, chips, or dullness before installing the beater assembly — Taylor's manual instructs to 
replace scraper blades that are nicked or damaged
, and specifically to 
be certain that scraper blades are properly attached to the helix
 before installing.
- **Check the rear shell bearing** for signs of wear or leakage — called out directly in Taylor's regular maintenance checks, and it's the same spot we identified as a hidden buildup/wear point for the drive coupling.
- **Confirm the mix hopper cover is properly seated** — a simple check, but Taylor's own troubleshooting guide lists 
the mix hopper cover is not in position
 as an actual fault condition with a specific fix (place the cover in position).
- **Inspect o-rings and seals** (door, beater shaft) for visible wear, flattening, or cracking before assembly, and lubricate properly — Taylor's guide notes 
inadequate lubrication of draw valve o-rings
 and 
using the wrong type of lubricant
 as documented causes of downstream problems.

### Daily — During operation

- **Listen for the beater motor** — new grinding, straining, or bogging sounds are early warning signs of the exact strain that later shows up as BEATER OVERLOAD.
- **Spot-check product consistency/texture** at each draw — density changes can flag both viscosity/overrun drift and beater strain before an overload trip occurs.
- **Note hopper/barrel temperature readouts** if your display shows them — catching temperature drift early can flag both HPCO-adjacent refrigeration issues and viscosity-driven beater strain.

### Weekly

- **Condenser visual check** — even outside the monthly cleaning cadence, a quick look for dust/lint buildup between full cleanings catches problems before they progress to a full HPCO trip. Taylor's own manual instructs operators to 
check the auxiliary storage condenser for accumulation of dirt and lint
, noting plainly that 
dirty
 condensers cause problems.
- **Clearance check** — confirm nothing has been pushed against the machine, since the manual specifies 
a minimum of 6 in. (152 mm) airspace is required
 on both sides for proper airflow.

### Monthly

- **Scraper blade replacement or close inspection** — matches the quarterly-to-monthly replacement window we discussed earlier, tightened to monthly if you're running high volume.
- **Condenser cleaning** — the baseline interval established earlier.
- **Drive coupling and rear bearing area cleaning** — specifically to catch the mix/lubricant buildup that's easy to miss in routine barrel cleaning.

### Log it, don't just check it

Given your specific situation — an overload that recurred for days before you dug into it — the single highest-value change isn't necessarily a new task, it's **writing down what you observe daily**, even when nothing trips. A simple log of "blades looked fine," "condenser had some buildup, cleaned it," "beater sounded a little rough" gives you a timeline the next time something faults, so you're not reconstructing history after the fact the way we've had to do this week. That log is also exactly what a Taylor service tech would want to see if this ever escalates to a service call.

**One practical suggestion:** since you now have a working amp-clamp habit from this week's troubleshooting, consider adding a **quick idle amp check** to your weekly (not daily — this is more wear-and-tear than urgent-fault-driven) routine. A slow upward drift in idle amps over weeks would give you weeks of advance warning before the next overload trip, rather than finding out only once it's already tripping.
